item.title: Gemini 4 AI Agents Win Minecraft Ender Dragon Battle
item.description:
Source: Engadget, Gizmodo Original headline: Google's Gemini 4 AI Agents Achieve First End-to-End Minecraft Victory
Google's Gemini 4 AI agents defeated the Ender Dragon in Minecraft without human intervention. Four agents, operating independently yet coordinating through in-game chat and shared memory, completed the task in 27.23 hours. The process involved writing 2,783 JavaScript programs, exchanging 229 messages, and experiencing 605 deaths during gameplay. A fifth 'Observer' agent monitored the session to ensure compliance and generate live reports. The experiment cost $810 at Gemini's list price or $1,620 at the standard rate, according to Google researchers. Gizmodo noted the cost was approximately $520 in tokens, highlighting pricing discrepancies. The agents used the open-source Mineflayer library to control in-game characters, executing tasks through code rather than direct input. Researchers emphasized the agents developed emergent behaviors, such as assigning roles like tool-making, food gathering, and portal construction, without explicit instructions beyond the shared goal. The achievement demonstrates AI's potential to handle complex, long-horizon tasks requiring multi-agent coordination, similar to real-world software engineering challenges. While the victory marks a milestone, researchers acknowledged the agents' frequent failures, noting success required maintaining a coherent plan across thousands of steps over an extended period.

item.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Hackers breached OpenCode's online platform, OpenCode Console, exposing API keys for 1.4% of users. The attack, described as a large-scale distillation breach, allowed unauthorized access to AI services like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, leading to charges exceeding $1,000 on some accounts. OpenCode notified affected users via email, urging them to revoke and replace exposed keys. Anthropic and Google blocked the leaked keys, while OpenAI collaborated with OpenCode to refund impacted customers. The breach was confined to the Console, not the open-source app or command-line tool, according to co-founder Dax Raad. Attackers attempted to infiltrate systems for 48 hours, forcing OpenCode to run AI defensive agents continuously. Safety filters in AI models hindered analysis, prompting the team to access OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program for vetted models. The incident mirrors similar challenges faced by Hugging Face, which encountered blocked analysis attempts by AI models during a security test. Security researchers criticize inconsistent guardrails, pushing some toward foreign open-weight models. The breach coincided with OpenCode’s release of GLM-5.3-Flash, a model with cybersecurity capabilities comparable to restricted-access systems. OpenCode has not disclosed how attackers gained access or the full impact of the breach, which remains ongoing. The incident adds to a wave of AI-enabled cyberattacks, including a recent report of China-based hackers using AI tools to target South Korean banks and unauthorized AI agents infiltrating Indian systems.

item.title: Rivian CEO predicts autonomy will enable new vehicle designs
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Rivian’s CEO says autonomy will enable ‘dramatically different’ vehicle designs
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe claims autonomy will enable 'dramatically different' vehicle designs beyond the company’s current SUVs and trucks. At TechCrunch Disrupt, he argued that self-driving technology opens new design possibilities for personally owned autonomous vehicles, allowing for 'radically different experiences.' Scaringe emphasized that autonomy could reshape transportation, though he acknowledged that most U.S. driving—95% of miles—remains done in privately owned vehicles, even with Level 4 autonomy. Rivian is advancing its driver-assistance system, aiming for 'point-to-point navigation' by year-end, and plans to deploy full autonomy in robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV via Uber. The company faces challenges scaling production of the R2 and refining self-driving software, which it recently reworked. While past autonomous vehicle concepts like Mercedes’ pod-like designs or Hyundai’s leg-equipped cars never materialized, Scaringe cites progress in robotaxis and EV component costs as reasons for renewed optimism. He hinted at a future R4 model, calling it 'cool' and 'great,' but declined to reveal details. Rivian’s push for autonomy comes as it seeks to reverse years of losses and establish itself as a major EV player.

item.title: Unicode domains enable persistent typo-squatting attacks
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Typo-squatting attacks with major domains are still viable
Unicode domain names enable typo-squatting attacks by allowing visually similar characters across alphabets. The IETF's decision to permit Unicode in domain names sparked concerns about security risks, as attackers can create deceptive websites with misspelled URLs resembling legitimate domains. Chromium browser employs advanced rules to detect such threats, but edge cases persist. Researchers demonstrated how domains like 'аррӏө.com' evade detection by using Cyrillic characters not included in Chromium's 29-character blacklist. While Chromium caught 64.1% of attempts in a 2020 study, other browsers like Firefox and Safari lag behind. The 'ө' character in 'аррӏө.com' bypasses checks because it isn't in the restricted list, highlighting the challenge of creating a universal solution. Domain registries enforce character rules for TLDs, but these measures are insufficient. HIBS advises companies to register lookalike domains and promote passkey authentication, which ties credentials to specific domains, preventing login to spoofed sites. With over 173,000 Unicode characters available, the problem remains complex, requiring ongoing vigilance from browser developers and registries.

item.title: Paid antivirus is unnecessary for most PC users in 2026
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
Windows Defender Antivirus has become reliable enough to replace paid antivirus suites for basic protection. Microsoft Defender, included in Windows 11, detected 100% of threats in 2026 tests, matching industry averages. It automatically scans files and updates without user intervention. Paid suites like Norton 360 Deluxe and Malwarebytes offer additional features such as VPNs, parental controls, and ransomware protection, but these extras are often unnecessary for most users. Performance impacts from third-party software, like a 15% drop in Cyberpunk 2077 frame rates during scans, may deter adoption. Free tools like Microsoft Edge's SmartScreen and Malwarebytes' free scanner provide sufficient coverage for standard threats. Experts advise against paying for antivirus out of habit, noting that Microsoft's built-in protection is sufficient for most users. Paid subscriptions often include redundant features and bloatware, while free alternatives offer comparable security. Users should consider paid suites only if they need specific extras like advanced scam detection or cross-device family protection.

item.title: Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Homeland Security has prohibited federal civilian agencies from using DeepSeek products. The Department of Homeland Security issued a directive through the Federal Register, citing risks of sensitive data transfer to the Chinese government and potential malware or security vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's models. The ban applies to all federal civilian agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency and Federal Communications Commission, requiring them to remove existing DeepSeek products and exclude the company from future contracts. The order follows the release of DeepSeek's latest model, V4.1-Flash-1017, which the company claims is more advanced. This marks another instance of U.S. government scrutiny of DeepSeek, which has faced prior restrictions, including a proposed congressional bill last year to ban its AI chatbot from government devices. DHS emphasized that DeepSeek's technology could compromise national security by enabling data exfiltration to China. The agency's actions align with broader concerns over foreign influence in AI development, particularly as DeepSeek's cost-effective models increasingly compete with U.S. alternatives like ChatGPT and Gemini.

item.title: Feynman's Vision of Miniaturization Faces Physical Limits
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: How far can we push computing?
Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture on miniaturization envisioned computing at the atomic scale, but physical limits now constrain progress. Scaling laws like Moore’s Law, which tracked transistor density, have slowed, while Dennard scaling—where smaller transistors used less power—ended around 2004. Hyperscalers now spend over $700 billion annually on data centers, relying on brute-force scaling rather than innovation. Other laws, such as Koomey’s and Kryder’s, also show diminishing returns. Feynman’s own challenges, like shrinking text to fit on a pinhead, were eventually met in 1985 using electron-beam lithography. The first transistor, created by Jack Kilby in 1958, marked the start of Moore’s Law, which predicted doubling transistor counts every two years. However, the cost-minimizing sweet spot for manufacturing transistors has shifted, slowing progress. Today, computing performance relies on system scaling—more chips, memory, and power—rather than shrinking transistors. AI training compute has doubled every six months since 2010, outpacing Moore’s Law. Despite these limits, computing still sits far from fundamental physical constraints. Seth Lloyd’s research explores how far miniaturization can go, with transistor density growing 10 orders of magnitude since the 1940s and energy efficiency improving 17 orders of magnitude. The industry now faces a trade-off between incremental improvements and breakthroughs that could redefine computing’s future.

item.title: Chinese Hacker Uses AI to Breach Over 100 Company Websites
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware, Gizmodo Original headline: Chinese Hacker Exploits AI Agents to Breach Over 100 Company Websites
A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to breach over 100 company websites, targeting businesses in the U.S., Canada, Australia, and Japan. The attack, which began in late September 2026, leveraged the open-source AI platform Cairn, combining models like China’s DeepSeek and Anthropic’s Claude Code. The hacker deployed AI agents to scan for vulnerabilities and execute attacks with minimal oversight, using fewer than 100 Chinese characters to instruct the agents. Over 1,200 websites were targeted, though only about 10% of attempts succeeded. Security researcher Snorre Fagerland noted the sophistication of the tactics, including AI agents identifying public-facing control panels, exploiting weaknesses, and executing malicious commands. 'It's not script kiddie stuff,' Fagerland told Reuters, emphasizing the advanced nature of the attacks. Some breaches resulted in stolen data, including credit card information and attempts to access cryptocurrency exchanges. NorForge estimated the campaign cost approximately $5,000 in token usage, or about $50 per successful breach. The exposed infrastructure of Cairn allowed researchers to observe the hacker’s activities, including prompt exchanges between the attacker and AI agents. The platform’s creator, @le1xia0, stated the tool was not designed for hacking and that its misuse was unintended. SharkNinja confirmed the attack only affected a product support site, but other breaches raised concerns about potential widespread data theft. The incident highlights the growing threat of AI-powered cyberattacks, as hackers increasingly rely on automation to scale operations with minimal effort.

item.title: Google AI extends fusion math solutions, challenges 59-year conjecture
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: 'It’s over, AI won': Google Gemini 4 Argon shatters 59-year-old nuclear fusion conjecture in just a few hours
Google’s Gemini 4 Argon AI helped researchers extend mathematical solutions to a 59-year-old conjecture about magnetic fields in fusion reactors. The work builds on earlier research that challenged physicist Harold Grad’s 1967 conjecture about equilibrium conditions in three-dimensional magnetic fields. University of Maryland researcher Matt Landreman and collaborators previously published exact solutions contradicting Grad’s theory, using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra Pro. However, those solutions relied on a geometric symmetry, leaving gaps in configurations without that property. Gemini 4 Argon, deployed via Google’s Antigravity environment, explored Landreman’s work and identified ways to remove the symmetry restriction, generating new mathematical configurations. These solutions provide additional reference cases for testing magnetic confinement simulations. The AI accelerated the search for solutions but did not replace the need for human verification. Researchers confirmed the mathematical consistency of the new configurations, though the work remains focused on advancing theoretical models rather than achieving commercial fusion. The study highlights AI’s role in tackling complex calculations but emphasizes that engineering challenges in fusion remain unresolved.

item.title: DLSS 5 modders report 90% performance boost on unsupported games
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Official DLSS 5 running on unsupported games delivers up to 90% better performance than the leaked version
Modders have extracted and are running the latest DLSS 5 version on unsupported games, showing significant performance improvements. The new Neural Rendering (NR) model, part of the 310.9.16.0 DLSS build, outperforms the previous version by up to 40% in some tests. Gaming Optimized compared the new model to the old one, finding up to 90% better performance in The Witcher 3 when using DLSS 5 natively. Nvidia optimized the AI model to be 24% smaller, using 20% less VRAM at 4K and processing neural rendering workloads up to 2x faster. Unlike typical AI model improvements, which increase parameters and size, Nvidia focused on efficiency due to consumer GPUs' limited VRAM. The new DLL includes two Neural Rendering presets: Preset A (old model) and Preset B (new model). Modders use tools like RenoDX and OptiScaler to inject DLSS into the graphics pipeline and tweak settings. The community has also modified the runtime to support RTX 20-series GPUs, despite Nvidia's official plans to release DLSS 5 only for RTX 40-series. Nvidia has not announced support for RTX 30- or RTX 20-series cards, but modders have bypassed this limitation through unofficial methods.

item.title: Wi-Fi HaLow offers long-range IoT connectivity despite limited adoption
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: This forgotten Wi-Fi standard can reach nearly 10 miles, but it isn't for what you think
Wi-Fi HaLow, a long-range wireless standard using sub-GHz frequencies, can reach nearly 10 miles but is designed for IoT devices rather than consumer electronics. Published in 2017 under IEEE 802.11ah, it operates in 863–868MHz (Europe) or 902–928MHz (US) bands, offering better penetration through obstacles and longer range than 2.4GHz Wi-Fi. Morse Micro demonstrated a 1Mbps video call at 1.8 miles in San Francisco and 2Mbps at 9.9 miles in Joshua Tree National Park. The standard supports up to 8,191 devices on a single access point, though practical limits are lower. Its narrow 1MHz channels improve range but reduce throughput. While ideal for low-power IoT applications like sensors and smart bulbs, Wi-Fi HaLow faces adoption challenges due to limited consumer device support, higher costs, and competition from established protocols like Zigbee and LoRaWAN. ABI Research predicts over 100 million HaLow-enabled devices by 2029, but mainstream adoption remains uncertain without broader hardware support.

item.title: Amazon Launches TorchNeuron to Challenge Nvidia in AI Chip Market
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
Amazon Web Services released TorchNeuron, a tool enabling AI startups to deploy PyTorch-based applications on Amazon’s Trainium AI chip with minimal configuration changes. The tool challenges Nvidia’s dominance in AI hardware, as Nvidia’s CUDA software has long facilitated seamless integration of PyTorch apps with its GPUs. Amazon claims 85% of AI apps use PyTorch, and by adapting the framework, TorchNeuron allows developers to leverage Trainium without rewriting code. AWS argues its cloud infrastructure offers cost advantages, as Trainium handles both AI training and inference tasks, reducing expenses despite not offering the lowest per-token pricing. Colin Brace, AWS’s VP of Technology Software, emphasized that using AWS provides a unified platform for scaling, unlike competitors like CoreWeave or Nebius, which are tied to Nvidia hardware. Amazon also plans to contribute code to PyTorch to reduce its reliance on Nvidia-specific optimizations, aiming to make the framework more hardware-agnostic. Deepgram, an AI voice app provider, cited cost savings after migrating to Trainium. If successful, Amazon’s efforts could weaken Nvidia’s lock on the AI chip market by decoupling PyTorch from Nvidia’s ecosystem, as Brace noted: 'The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.'

item.title: MLO on routers: What it is and whether to enable it
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What does MLO mean on your router and should you enable it?
Multi-Link Operation (MLO) is a feature in Wi-Fi 7 routers designed to allow simultaneous connections to multiple frequency bands, potentially improving internet speeds and stability. However, MLO remains unfulfilled in practice. The term refers to two implementations: Simultaneous Transit and Receive mode, which uses multiple radios to connect to multiple bands, and Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio mode, which uses a single radio to switch between bands without interruptions. A February 2026 report by Rtings found no Wi-Fi 7 routers supported the full multi-radio version of MLO. Compatibility issues persist as Wi-Fi 7 devices cannot work with older Wi-Fi 6 or earlier hardware, limiting MLO benefits. Devices without Wi-Fi 7 compatibility cannot use MLO, risking network instability. Experts advise against enabling MLO unless a full Wi-Fi 7 setup is in place with compatible devices. Router settings for MLO vary by brand, with some models like ASUS enabling it by default. Users are encouraged to check settings to determine the optimal configuration.

item.title: Netgear Router Lights: Meaning and Troubleshooting Guide
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
Netgear routers feature multiple indicator lights that signal device status and connectivity. The power light indicates the router's operational state: solid green or white means the device is on and ready; amber signifies startup or firmware updates; blinking white suggests firmware corruption. The internet connection light shows connectivity status: off means no modem link, solid green indicates a stable connection, and amber signals an Ethernet cable is detected. Wi-Fi traffic is indicated by a light with two curves: off means Wi-Fi is disabled, solid white shows active radios, and blinking white indicates data transfer. Additional lights track 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands, with colors reflecting connection speed. USB ports have lights showing device status: off means no connection, blinking indicates a device is attempting to connect, and solid green means a device is active. Ethernet ports use color-coded lights to show connection speed: white/green for 1 Gbps, amber for slower speeds. A WPS light indicates connection progress: off means no connection, blinking shows setup in progress, and solid green confirms success. For Orbi mesh systems, front lights show connection strength: solid blue for strong links, amber for weak, and magenta for no backhaul. Back lights indicate power and firmware status: solid green means powered on, amber indicates rebooting, and pulsing amber signals firmware updates. If a router is unresponsive, restarting or resetting may resolve issues.

item.title: AI Coding Expands Security Risks in Software Development
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Why AI coding is widening the software security gap
AI coding assistants are now widely used, with about half of committed code in organizations being AI-generated. While these systems produce syntactically correct code at a 99.9% rate, security performance is significantly lower, with an average pass rate of 56%. This means 44% of AI-generated code introduces known vulnerabilities, making software vulnerabilities the top breach entry point at 31%, surpassing stolen credentials. Chris Wysopal, Chief Security Evangelist at Veracode, argues that security must be integrated into AI-assisted development from the start. AI models trained on historical code, including insecure patterns, can reproduce these risks at scale. Organizations cannot control all training data but can select models with better security outcomes. The strongest model tested achieved a 68% security pass rate, while most others scored between 50% and 53%. Security must be part of the development lifecycle, with testing and policies enforced. AI-generated code may pass functional tests but still contain vulnerabilities, creating misplaced confidence. Context matters in verification, as models perform better on some vulnerabilities like SQL injection (83% pass rate) than others like cross-site scripting (15%). AI-native analysis can detect risks in pull requests, but independent testing remains critical. As AI accelerates software development, security teams face growing backlogs of unresolved vulnerabilities, with 82% of organizations affected by security debt. Prioritizing remediation based on exploitability and business impact is essential. AI-powered fixes can help but must be validated to avoid introducing new risks. Leaders must treat AI’s security implications as a shift in the software operating model, ensuring verification is built into workflows and risks are managed proactively. Organizations that adapt their practices to align security with AI adoption will succeed in mitigating risks before code reaches production.

item.title: Tolan Raises $30M for AI Companion App
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
Tolan, an AI companion app designed to assist users with daily tasks, relationships, and emotional support, has raised $30 million in new funding. The round, led by Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, brings the startup’s total raised to over $120 million and pushes its valuation beyond $268 million, according to PitchBook. Tolan’s app features a cartoonish character that guides users through to-dos and conversations, generating revenue through tiered memberships. The company reports annual recurring revenue in the double-digit millions, with over 250,000 active users and 70 million conversations in the past year. Approximately 70% of users are women, and 40% are parents. The app has gained traction among neurodivergent users seeking structured support. Tolan contrasts with failed competitors like Friend, whose AI companion faced public backlash for being ‘cringe,’ and Character.AI, which filed for bankruptcy after its founder left for Google. The startup now faces competition from newer AI agents that focus on task planning and organization, such as Meta’s Muse. Tolan must also navigate legal risks tied to AI-driven emotional support, as lawsuits allege chatbots contributed to user suicides. The company’s success highlights growing demand for AI tools that balance helpfulness with relatability in a crowded market.

item.title: Apple's Image Playground app creates custom images and Genmoji
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
Apple's Image Playground app generates custom images using Apple Intelligence, allowing users to create and modify visuals for personal use or sharing. Launched in December 2024, the app integrates with Messages, Keynote, and Freeform, enabling real-time image creation without switching apps. To use it, users need an iPhone 15 Pro/Pro Max, iPhone 16 or later with Apple Intelligence enabled, iPads with M1 chip or later, or Macs with M1 chip. The latest iOS 27 update adds features like describing visual styles in natural language, modifying existing images via touch gestures, and creating Contact Posters or Lock Screen wallpapers. Users can start with text prompts, select pre-defined styles like animation or sketch, or use a photo as a reference. For example, selecting a face from a photo allows customization, such as turning a user into an astronaut. Images can be saved, shared, or converted into Genmoji. The app also supports using a taken photo as a base for new images, with options to tweak details through touch interactions. Updates enhance flexibility, letting users refine creations with both text and manual adjustments.

item.title: Roku Star Button Functions Vary by Context and Device
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What is the star button for on your Roku remote?
The star button on Roku remotes serves different functions depending on the device context. On the home screen, pressing the star while an app is highlighted in Quick Access removes it from the section. In the full app list, it provides options to view app version/build numbers, move channels, remove them, rate, provide feedback, check for updates, or rename external devices like game consoles. During streaming, the star button opens a sidebar with viewing options such as adjusting image quality, setting sleep timers, enabling closed captioning, changing volume modes, and app-specific settings. Roku TVs offer more options than streaming boxes. The star button also activates a text-to-speech screen reader (available only in the U.S.) by pressing it four times rapidly. Accessibility settings, including speech rate and volume adjustments, require navigating to the Settings page. The feature is supported on Roku Streaming Stick and Streaming Stick+ devices.

item.title: 2.5G Ethernet ports offer faster local network speeds but require compatible hardware
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What's the point of the 2.5G Ethernet port on your router?
2.5G Ethernet ports on routers provide speeds up to 2.5 Gbps, compared to standard 1 Gbps ports. These ports, labeled as 2.5G or 2.5GbE, require compatible devices, Cat5e or newer cables, and an ISP plan of at least 2.5 Gbps to fully utilize their speed. While faster internet plans benefit from the upgrade, local network tasks like NAS backups can leverage the full 2.5 Gbps speed even with slower internet. However, most users see diminishing returns beyond 1 Gbps, making the upgrade more relevant for heavy data transfers or cloud backups rather than everyday activities like streaming or gaming. The primary advantage is reduced load times for large file transfers, but the benefit depends on matching hardware and network conditions.

item.title: Laplace Intelligence Uses AI to Test Physical Robots and Self-Driving Cars Before Deployment
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
Laplace Intelligence, a startup based in Ann Arbor, is developing AI-driven red-teaming tools to stress-test robotics and self-driving cars before deployment. CEO Howie Sun emphasized the risks of physical AI failing in the real world, citing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident as a cautionary example. The company uses high-fidelity simulations grounded in real-world data, such as Nvidia’s Cosmos platform, to recreate environments like Arizona highways and Paris pedestrian crossings. These simulations, combined with AI agents that probe for weaknesses, aim to ensure safety in autonomous systems. Sun and co-founder Henry Liu, a former PhD adviser, founded Laplace after publishing research in Nature in 2023, which attracted interest from autonomous vehicle companies. Laplace’s technology generates edge cases by analyzing news, police reports, and real-time data like traffic patterns from TomTom. The startup is already working with clients including Bot Auto, a Texas-based trucking firm, and a major Japanese automaker, as well as partners in smart city and humanoid robotics projects. While competing with firms like Applied Intuition, Sun argues Laplace’s approach of using AI to test AI represents a new paradigm in physical AI safety. The company is also participating in TechCrunch Disrupt’s Startup Battlefield 200, aiming to scale and secure funding. Sun called their methodology a 'dynamic interactive testing process' that could become a competitive advantage.

item.title: MIT Engineers Create Soft 3D Shape-Sensing Skin for Gaming and VR
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: MIT engineers build soft 3D shape-sensing skin for gaming and VR
MIT engineers developed a soft, wearable shape-sensing sheet using optical waveguide arrays to track 3D movement with sub-centimeter accuracy. The technology, described in a paper published in *Advanced Intelligent Systems*, employs flexible rubber cores and black-dyed cladding in optical fibers to detect bending in both directions. A zig-zag arrangement of 14 waveguides, each 160 mm long, embedded in a silicone sheet, enables directional sensing by altering light loss based on bending orientation. The system uses LEDs and light sensors to measure shape, with an algorithm translating data into 3D reconstructions processed in MATLAB. Lab tests showed error rates under 0.3 cm when up to three waveguides were disabled, though accuracy dropped to 1 cm with five disabled. Real-world tests on 3D-printed molds achieved root-mean-square distances of 0.28–0.45 cm. The sheet remains functional even when damaged, though fibers are thicker than ideal for garments. Qifan Yu, a graduate student on the team, noted the system’s accuracy matches existing rigid-sensor designs. MIT assistant professor Kaitlyn Becker highlighted potential applications in physical therapy, VR, and robotics. Future work aims to reduce fiber thickness, improve resolution with more layers, and integrate force sensing. The technology could enable safer, more responsive wearable interfaces for gaming, teleoperation, and smart garments.

item.title: Burger King Japan breach exposes 11.18 million customer records
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Whopper of a data breach sees Burger King Japan expose over 11 million customer records
Burger King Japan confirmed a data breach exposing 11.18 million customer records through its mobile app platform. The compromised data included personal details such as names, dates of birth, genders, email addresses, phone numbers, and order histories. Payment information was not accessed. The breach occurred between October 2 and October 7, 2026, with unauthorized access identified on October 13, 2026. The company blocked the source and notified regulators, including the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). Burger King Japan stated no confirmed misuse of the data and apologized for the inconvenience. The breach follows similar incidents in 2024, including a Russian Burger King breach and a Mindbox attack that exposed customer data. Mindbox, a marketing platform used by Burger King, reported the attack was its first major security incident, involving unauthorized access to sensitive data. The company implemented stricter access controls, two-factor authentication, and revised development processes to prevent future breaches. Burger King Russia is listed on Have I Been Pwned, but Japan’s breach is not yet reported there. The incident highlights vulnerabilities in third-party supply chain attacks, which often affect multiple companies using shared tools.
