item.title: Video doorbell motion detection ranges vary by brand and model
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
Video doorbell motion detection ranges vary by brand and model. Ring states its devices can detect motion up to 30 feet (9 meters), but larger objects like cars may trigger alerts beyond that range. However, maximum ranges are not guaranteed and depend on factors like camera sensitivity, mounting location, and environmental conditions. eufy's Video Doorbell detects horizontal motion up to 15 feet and vertical motion up to 5 feet. Arlo's second-generation model has a 13-foot range, while Essential models reach 16 feet. TELUS claims its doorbell works best within 8 feet and requires continuous movement for seven seconds to trigger alerts. Motion detection types also differ: passive infrared (PIR) sensors are more sensitive to side-to-side movement, while pixel difference analysis (PDA) compares video frames for changes. Some devices combine PIR with video analytics. Users can adjust motion sensitivity and set detection zones to focus on specific areas. Environmental factors like moving trees, sunlight, and shadows can cause false alerts, as noted by Ring. Battery-powered models like Google's Nest Doorbell consume more power in high-traffic areas, and users can adjust activity zones or camera angles to reduce unnecessary triggers. Ring recommends mounting doorbells 48 inches above ground. Subscription plans affect features like viewing recorded video or distinguishing between people, vehicles, and packages, but they do not expand physical motion detection range.

item.title: Expensive Wi-Fi 7 Routers May Deliver Slower Speeds
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Why your expensive Wi-Fi 7 router could be delivering slower speeds
Wi-Fi 7 routers may deliver slower speeds than expected despite promises of up to 46 Gbps. Users report confusion over unmet speed expectations, with online forums highlighting troubleshooting efforts. Key factors include router placement, device count, and compatibility. The Wi-Fi Alliance launched Wi-Fi 7 in 2024, offering lower latency and congestion management for high-density environments. Adoption reached 7.2% by early 2026, up from 1.8% a year prior. Poor placement, such as near drywall, can degrade signals by causing signal bouncing. Moving routers to open spaces or three feet from corners may improve performance. Homes often have over 20 connected devices, requiring routers with fast processors, dual frequency bands, and sufficient ISP bandwidth. Wi-Fi 7’s multi-link operation (MLO) allows devices to use multiple bands simultaneously for faster, more reliable connections. Users should check if slowdowns occur during peak usage or consistently, adjusting settings accordingly.

item.title: Google Launches AI Content Detection Tool
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
Google has launched SynthID Detector, a tool allowing users to check if an image, video, or audio file was generated by AI. The tool scans for imperceptible watermarks embedded by Google's Gemini AI model and SynthID partners like OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, and Apple. Users can access the tool by uploading files to SynthID.com, with results provided within seconds. The service, available to all after a 2025 limited rollout, offers a simple yes/no response about detected watermarks. However, it cannot identify AI-generated content without SynthID labels, such as media from Meta's tools. Google claims its watermarks persist even after edits, though no tool is foolproof against determined manipulation. The detector requires a Google, OpenAI, or Apple account and limits users to 10 checks per day. While SynthID Detector is more reliable than other tools like Meta's Content Seal, which had accuracy issues, no universal AI detection method exists. Researchers have developed their own tools, but they are not publicly available. The tool helps verify content but does not analyze media for AI-generated patterns beyond existing watermarks.

item.title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good. Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study. But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.” If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

item.title: Foldable Phones Evolve Toward Mainstream Adoption
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: From the Royole FlexPai to the iPhone Duo: How the modern foldable phone has evolved
Foldable phones have evolved significantly since their early days, with companies like Royole, Samsung, and Huawei pioneering the technology. The Royole FlexPai, unveiled in 2019, was the first commercially available foldable smartphone but faced criticism for its durability and design. Samsung's Galaxy Fold, also released in 2019, encountered widespread issues with screen damage due to a protective plastic layer, leading to recalls and design revisions. Huawei's Mate X, which folded outward, showcased an elegant design but struggled with screen fragility and U.S. market restrictions. Over the next few years, manufacturers focused on improving screen durability, with Samsung introducing ultra-thin glass and IP ratings, while Oppo's Find N reduced visible creases. Pricing also dropped, with models like the Galaxy Z Flip 3 and Motorola Razr making foldables more accessible. Apple entered the market in 2026 with the iPhone Duo, a dual-screen device with a 7.6-inch internal display and 5.4-inch external screen, priced at $1,999. Analysts predict the iPhone Duo could sell 6 million units in 2026, signaling foldables' potential mainstream adoption. The evolution of foldable phones, marked by iterative improvements and overcoming technical hurdles, positions them as a viable alternative to traditional smartphones.

item.title: Starlink offers two $55 plans with different data caps and speeds
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Starlink has two $55 plans that are wildly different — here's how
Starlink offers two $55 plans with different data caps and speeds. The Residential plan is for fixed locations with unlimited data, while the Roam plan is for mobile users with data limits. Residential tiers provide 100 Mbps, 200 Mbps, or 400 Mbps speeds with no data caps. Roam tiers offer 100GB, 300GB, or unlimited data with speeds up to 300 Mbps. Both plans include a 30-day trial with a full refund option. Starlink's fair use policy may reduce speeds during high congestion or peak hours. Users should check coverage maps for available speeds. Residential plans include free professional installation, while Roam requires a Starlink Mini dish. The Roam plan is best for RVs, nomads, and international travelers. Data caps on Roam plans throttle speeds after monthly limits are reached. Residential plans are suited for long-term home use, while Roam is designed for mobility. Both plans start at $55 but vary in data allowances and speed tiers.

item.title: Study highlights rising battery emissions and reduction strategies
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Batteries help reduce emissions, but how do we reduce their emissions?
A study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne examines emissions from lithium-ion batteries, which are critical for the energy transition. Current emissions from battery production account for 0.18 percent of annual greenhouse gas emissions, but could rise by 10 times by 2050 as battery demand grows. The research highlights that while batteries help reduce emissions by enabling electrification, their own production remains a concern. Strategies to cut emissions include using less energy-intensive materials, improving manufacturing efficiency, and expanding recycling to reuse battery components with lower energy demands than mining. The study also evaluates demand-side solutions, such as reducing the number of batteries needed, to avoid emissions entirely. Researchers used life-cycle projections for electric vehicles and energy storage through 2050, incorporating regional differences in demand and electricity generation based on International Energy Agency scenarios. The analysis compares emissions savings against a future with more batteries, higher recycling rates, and a cleaner grid, emphasizing the need for systemic changes in both production and usage to mitigate environmental impact.

item.title: Fiber and cable internet differ in speed, reliability, and availability
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
Fiber-optic and cable internet differ in speed, reliability, and availability. Fiber uses light through glass strands for faster speeds and better reliability, while cable relies on electricity via copper cores, making it more prone to interference. Fiber offers higher bandwidth and symmetrical upload/download speeds, but cable is more widely available. The Fiber Broadband Association reports 60% of U.S. households have fiber access, compared to 96.9% with fixed broadband at 100/20 Mbps. Fiber connections typically start at 100 Mbps, with plans up to 50 Gbps, while cable speeds range from 300 Mbps to 1 Gbps. Hybrid fiber-coaxial networks provide 1 Gbps downloads but lower uploads. Pricing varies: Google Fiber offers 1 Gbps for $70/month, while Xfinity’s hybrid cable plans start at $45/month for 300 Mbps. Fiber requires an Optical Network Terminal (ONT), whereas cable users may need separate modems or gateways. Bundled TV and phone services are common with cable. Wireless 5G is an alternative but has higher latency. Both options require proper router setup to avoid slow Wi-Fi, with Ethernet connections reducing latency for gaming and video calls.

item.title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
ReactOS, an open-source Windows alternative, has achieved a major milestone by enabling direct installation on NTFS drives. Phoronix reports the development clears a long-standing barrier, bringing the project closer to beta status. Previously, ReactOS required FAT32 partitions for installations, limiting its compatibility with modern Windows systems. NTFS, a Microsoft filesystem introduced in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1 and standardized in Windows XP in 2001, is now supported. The update aligns with ReactOS’s goal of binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003. However, the new NTFS driver lacks caching, journaling, and security features, resulting in inferior performance. ReactOS developers warned of potential undiscovered bugs in their X announcement, advising users to proceed with caution despite the progress. The milestone marks significant advancement but underscores ongoing challenges in replicating the Windows environment.

item.title: Apple HomeView's Square Screen Faces Streaming Challenges
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: The Apple HomeView's Most Unique Feature Might Be Its Biggest Mistake
Apple's HomeView smart display features a square screen instead of the standard widescreen format used by competitors like Amazon and Google. During a demo at Apple's 'Welcome Home' event, the device was praised for its feature-rich design and readiness to compete with existing smart home hubs. However, the square 1:1 aspect ratio poses challenges for video streaming, forcing content to shrink significantly and resulting in heavy letterboxing on top and bottom. Vertical video platforms like Instagram Reels and TikTok also face compromises, though the square format handles vertical feeds slightly better than traditional widescreens. Apple's design choice appears to balance household needs, offering passable widescreen video for adults and usable social feeds for children, with some black bars tolerated. The square screen aligns the HomeView with Apple Watch and CarPlay, using a hybrid operating system combining elements of watchOS and CarPlay. While native streaming options are limited at launch, Safari and AirPlay support allow content streaming. The square format also functions well for non-video tasks like smart home controls, calendars, and recipe cards, with step-by-step modes and integrated widgets working seamlessly. Apple's automatic image cropping enhances photos on the square screen, though Google's Nest Hub achieves a similar effect on a widescreen panel. The design choice reflects Apple's strategy to prioritize utility over conventional form factors, despite potential drawbacks in video playback.

item.title: Three Linux distros abandoned by creators
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: 3 Linux distros that ruled the world until they were suddenly abandoned by their creators
CentOS, Mandrake Linux, and CrunchBang Linux each reached widespread popularity before their creators abandoned them. CentOS, a free rebuild of Red Hat Enterprise Linux, was replaced by CentOS Stream in 2020, ending its eight-year support cycle. Red Hat’s decision left administrators upset, prompting forks like Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux to fill the gap. Mandrake Linux, launched in 1998 by Gaël Duval, became a favorite for new users with its user-friendly installer and KDE desktop. Financial struggles and a legal dispute over its name led to its rebranding as Mandriva Linux in 2005. By 2010, Mandriva faced layoffs and management changes, eventually liquidating in 2015. CrunchBang Linux, created in 2008 by Philip Newborough, offered a minimalist Debian-based system with a dark theme and low resource usage. Its 2015 discontinuation was met with community action, leading to projects like BunsenLabs. All three distros highlight how open-source projects can outlive their creators, with communities stepping in to sustain their legacy.

item.title: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion. The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price. Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation. Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

item.title: Startup Tests Subsea Geothermal Power Near Underwater Volcano
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
The world's first subsea geothermal power plant demonstration occurred near Axial Seamount, an active underwater volcano in the northeast Pacific Ocean. The three-week test, conducted by Seattle-based startup Endurance Energy in September, involved a 3-ton prototype that generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity. The test aimed to prove the technical viability of harnessing geothermal energy underwater, targeting markets like Pacific island nations seeking alternatives to fossil fuel imports. Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, noted the deep ocean provides 'unlimited cold seawater for cooling' and 'weight keeps the system and the well pressurized,' enabling compact plant designs. However, challenges include higher installation and operational costs compared to land-based projects. Roland Horne, a Stanford University professor, acknowledged the approach is 'technically feasible' but warned it would be 'more expensive than to do it on land.' The deployment required a subsea lander drill to drill two holes at a depth of about 5,000 feet (1,524 meters), exceeding 2.5 times the height of the One World Trade Center building in New York City. Endurance Energy now faces the task of demonstrating consistent underwater operations and cost-effectiveness for commercialization.

item.title: Arctic Fires Accelerate Permafrost Thaw, Releasing Carbon
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
A wildfire in Alaska's boreal forest in 2021 accelerated permafrost thaw, exposing ancient carbon stores and triggering concerns about climate feedback loops. Researchers from the Alaska Fire Science Consortium, including Hilary Shook and Alison York, documented how the fire stripped away insulating moss and soil, allowing permafrost to thaw rapidly. Shook’s thaw probe revealed permafrost depths three times deeper than normal in burned areas, confirming the fire’s immediate impact. Scientists warn that intensifying Arctic wildfires, fueled by climate change, are accelerating permafrost loss, which could release 80 billion tons of CO2 by 2100—more than half the carbon emissions from direct vegetation burning. Canada’s 2023 wildfires emitted more carbon than its fossil fuel emissions, highlighting the scale of the crisis. Researchers are exploring interventions like controlled burns and rapid fire suppression to mitigate emissions, though such measures face logistical and ethical challenges. The Woodwell Climate Research Center, along with the Polis Institute and Alaska Venture Fund, launched the North Fire initiative to study these strategies, citing a 2022 study showing fire suppression could be cost-effective compared to renewable energy projects. However, agencies like Alaska’s focus on protecting life and property, not global climate goals. Researchers argue that human-driven climate change has already altered fire patterns, creating a ‘massive blind spot’ in climate models. Despite growing urgency, balancing resource allocation and risk management remains contentious as permafrost thaw threatens to amplify global warming.

item.title: 80% of Americans Receive Fake Texts or Emails Weekly, Survey Finds
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Scam Fatigue Is Real: Our Survey Says 80% of Americans Get Fake Texts or Emails Every Week
A CNET Group survey of 1,000 Americans reveals 80% receive fake texts or emails weekly, with 75% facing spam calls at least once per week. Notification fatigue from constant alerts undermines ability to detect scams, making fraud more damaging than traditional viruses. Senior security writer Kim Key cited a case where a 77-year-old retired nurse lost $400,000 to an AI-driven impersonation scam. The survey found 29.4% of respondents received scam calls six times weekly, compared to 26.5% for scam emails and 18% for texts. Digital trust eroded by AI-generated messages, with 39.0% distrusting bank-related communications and 31.7% skeptical of celebrity endorsements. Only 16.4% believed most online content was authentic. Survey participants reported high scam anxiety, with 19% rating their worry at 10 on a 10-point scale. Nearly 60% had experienced scams in the past year, with credit card fraud, phishing, and payment app fraud being the top threats. The study underscores how persistent scamming tactics and AI advancements create a growing vulnerability for consumers.

item.title: Microsoft Warns AI Agents Pose Insider Threat Risks
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
Microsoft introduced new security features to protect enterprises from AI agents, framing them as potential insider threats. The company launched Guardian Agents, part of Project Perception, which includes red, blue, and green teams to simulate hacking, detection, and remediation. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned in a private blog that AI agents, like rogue employees, cannot be trusted, urging enterprises to separate control from model providers. He emphasized that "we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it." Hayete Gallot, Microsoft’s security chief, stated frontier models are unpredictable and lack organizational norms, making them risky despite not being malicious. Microsoft’s solution includes Guardian Agents, Microsoft Defender’s agent detection, and dynamic access controls requiring human approval for risky actions. The company also joined Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, which isolates agents in secure environments. Microsoft’s approach highlights growing industry concerns about AI agents as untrustworthy insiders, despite its own ties to OpenAI and Anthropic. The strategy aims to position Microsoft as a leader in agent security, offering tools to monitor and restrict AI behavior while distancing from model providers.

item.title: F-22 Pilot Commands Drone in Simulated Combat Test
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: F-22 Raptor pilot successfully demonstrates command of 'wingman' fighter drone in simulated combat
U.S. Air Force pilot successfully directed an Anduril YFQ-44A Fury drone during simulated combat, demonstrating command integration for the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program. The test, conducted by The Defense Watch, showed the pilot issuing tactical commands that the autonomous drone interpreted into flight maneuvers. The CCA initiative aims to integrate drones into fighter squadrons, allowing pilots to assign specific tasks to drones while focusing on primary missions like engaging enemy fighters. However, operational deployment remains years away, as the program must address challenges including defining the drone’s tactical autonomy, ensuring safe flight control, and testing weapons authorization. Additional hurdles involve evaluating performance under electronic interference, maintaining continuous operation during communication disruptions, and integrating drones into logistics, maintenance, and supply chain systems. The USAF views autonomous drones as a force multiplier, enabling a single pilot to command multiple aircraft at lower costs. While Sweden and China also explore similar concepts, the CCA focuses on air power rather than ground operations. The test marks progress but underscores the need for extensive testing before frontline deployment.

item.title: Flipkart Enters India's Food Delivery Market
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Walmart’s Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce company, is preparing to enter India’s food-delivery market, challenging the duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. The company is testing its food-delivery service internally, expanding the trial to over 8,000 employees and deploying a dedicated rider fleet through its logistics arm, Ekart. The service operates as a separate tab in Flipkart’s app, using restaurants from the government-backed ONDC network and direct partnerships. Flipkart plans a public launch by October, aiming to expand to five or six cities by year-end. The market, growing at 18-20% annually, is dominated by Zomato and Swiggy, which serve 85-95 million paying customers yearly. Flipkart’s approach differs from past entrants like Amazon and Google, which failed to gain traction. Sagar Daryani, president of the National Restaurant Association of India, noted the need for alternatives to reduce restaurant costs, citing Flipkart’s proposed 10% commission versus the 20-25% typical on existing platforms. He expects Flipkart to lower overall costs to 15-16% of order value. While new entrants may save customers ₹20-30 per order, Zomato and Swiggy could counter with deeper discounts. Flipkart’s move also comes amid uncertainty around its stock listing and intensifying competition in India’s e-commerce sector. The company has not commented on the matter.

item.title: TP-Link to Assemble Routers in U.S. Amid Foreign-Made Ban
item.description:
Source: PCMag, Engadget Original headline: TP-Link Partners with US Manufacturer to Assemble Routers Amid Foreign-Made Ban
TP-Link has partnered with Key Tronic Corporation to assemble Wi-Fi 8 routers in Mississippi under the U.S. foreign-made router ban. The agreement, signed in late 2023, aims to begin production at Key Tronic’s Corinth facility by 2027. TP-Link’s strategy includes a nearly $1 billion investment to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities, aligning with the Trump administration’s supply chain security goals. Steve Kovsky, TP-Link’s corporate affairs officer, noted the company still relies on overseas components like Qualcomm and Broadcom chipsets, a challenge shared across the industry. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) classifies all foreign-made routers as security risks, allowing existing inventory to remain on shelves but requiring companies to demonstrate U.S. manufacturing plans for exemptions. TP-Link submitted a detailed plan to regulators, including component and software origin breakdowns, and is seeking a temporary exemption. Other firms like Netgear and Asus have already received similar waivers. Kovsky emphasized TP-Link’s compliance efforts, citing FCC guidelines’ lack of clarity on exemption criteria. The success of the reshoring initiative depends on regulatory approval and domestic component availability. TP-Link’s partnership with Key Tronic represents one of the few public disclosures of a U.S.-based manufacturing push by a router provider since the ban was announced in March 2023.

item.title: ChatGPT Can Now Take Control of Your Chrome Tabs
item.description:
Source: PCMag
OpenAI's ChatGPT now allows users to control Chrome tabs through deeper browser integrations. The Chrome extension, which has read open tabs since July, now operates in Work mode to actively manage tabs. Features include filling out forms with user data before submission, sending messages, downloading files, and grouping tabs by topic. Users can tag Chrome directly in ChatGPT's web or desktop app by adding @Chrome to prompts or referencing specific tabs. The integration supports Chromium-based browsers like Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, but not Firefox or Safari. The feature is free for all ChatGPT plans, including the free tier. OpenAI previously retired its standalone browser, ChatGPT Atlas, in August but continues to expand browser capabilities. The update eliminates the need for the Side Chat panel, enabling tab-based context use across multiple browsers.

item.title: Russian Satellite Approaches US Spy Satellite Supporting Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware, Ars Technica Original headline: Russian Satellite Conducts Unsanctioned Rendezvous with US Commercial Satellite Supporting Ukraine
A Russian military satellite, Kosmos 2612, executed an unsanctioned maneuver to approach within 3 miles of the U.S.-operated commercial satellite ICEYE-X36, which supports Ukraine. The maneuver, described as the first known instance of such behavior in low-Earth orbit, brought the Russian satellite within 500 meters of ICEYE-X36 over the weekend, according to LeoLabs. The approach required significant fuel consumption, indicating deliberate intent, as noted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. ICEYE-X36, launched in March 2024, operates at 545 km in a sun-synchronous orbit and has provided Ukraine with imagery since 2022. The Russian satellite’s actions followed earlier maneuvers by Cosmos 2609, which passed within 2.5 km of ICEYE-X36 on May 26. By late September, Kosmos 2612 had adjusted its orbit through a series of burns between September 30 and October 16 to align with ICEYE-X36’s trajectory, as tracked by Dutch satellite expert Marco Langbroek. Jonathan McDowell, an astronomer, stated the satellite’s actions ‘remove any remaining doubt’ about its interest in ICEYE-X36. While close-proximity operations can have benign purposes, policymakers are urged to consider potential hostile intent. The incident mirrors past Russian activities, such as the 2020 maneuver by Cosmos 2543, which drew condemnation from the U.S. and U.K. The exact purpose of Kosmos 2612’s approach remains unclear, but the deliberate nature of the maneuvers has prompted calls for increased monitoring and a clear response to potential threats in space.
item.source: Latest from Tom's Hardware, Ars Technica

item.title: Claude Code AI detects crypto miner on overheating Mac
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Claude Code AI agent caught a crypto miner hiding on a developer’s overheating Mac
A developer using Claude Code to build a temperature monitor app discovered a crypto miner on their overheating Mac. The AI agent flagged the presence of xmrig, noting it was using 1175% CPU across roughly 12 cores, causing the Mac to run at 112 degrees Celsius. The malware, added to the startup roster on August 29, was likely responsible for the system’s excessive heat. UntilHEX, the developer, admitted the miner explained their Mac’s poor performance. Claude Code offered to clean the malware by stopping the startup item and moving files to a quarantine folder, though the developer had to manually delete one file due to access issues. A subsequent Malwarebytes scan confirmed the cleanup’s effectiveness. The incident highlights how AI tools can detect and mitigate malware, even as cryptomining exploits hardware resources.

item.title: Robot vacuums collect personal data, raising privacy concerns
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Robot vacuums have a major privacy problem you should be aware of
Robot vacuums collect personal data like floor maps, cleaning histories, and audio, raising privacy concerns. Cloud connectivity allows manufacturers to access user data, including room names, detected objects, and Wi-Fi details. A 2026 incident revealed a security flaw where user Sammy Azdoufal remotely controlled 7,000 vacuums due to a server error that failed to restrict access to his device. DJI fixed the issue with updates on February 10, 2026, but the flaw stemmed from inadequate security checks, not AI. Other risks include continuous data transmission, such as movement logs and environmental scans, even without cameras. Privacy policies often lack clarity, with companies burying terms in legalese. Matic is highlighted as a privacy-friendly option, using local processing and encrypted cloud sharing only with consent. Users are advised to enable strong passwords, two-factor authentication, and firmware updates. While privacy policies outline commitments, they don't guarantee security against breaches. Features like remote viewing should be disabled unless necessary. Manufacturers may still face vulnerabilities despite policy claims, emphasizing the need for proactive user safeguards.

item.title: Archer Aviation Completes California Air-Taxi Flight Tour
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Archer Aviation Touts Completion of ‘No Roads’ Air-Taxi Flight Tour of California
Archer Aviation completed a Northern California leg of its 'No Roads' air-taxi flight tour, showcasing its Midnight eVTOL aircraft. The four-passenger electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft flew from Oakland International Airport to nearby airports including Hayward, Mountain View, San Martin, and San Jose. A flight from Oakland to San Francisco’s Marina District took 10 minutes, compared to over an hour by car. Midnight reached speeds of 131mph during the tour, accumulating more than 200 flight miles over three days. The aircraft has a claimed 100-mile range and top speed of 150mph, using 12 rotors—six spinning vertically during takeoffs and landings, and six pivoting upright for powered flight. Archer also demonstrated conventional takeoffs and landings at an air show in Salinas, CA, in late September. The company plans further testing in Los Angeles to prepare for the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), aiming to operate air-taxi services during the 2028 Olympics in LA. Archer was named the 'Official Air Taxi Provider' for the games in May 2023 and has outlined plans for air-taxi networks in Miami and New York City. However, commercial operations require FAA type certification, which could take five to nine years. Archer applied for certification in March 2022 and claims to have completed three of four phases of the process.

item.title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June. Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company. Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round. We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

item.title: Slate Truck Uses Phone for OTA Updates Without Infotainment System
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Here's how the Slate truck gets software updates without built-in infotainment
The Slate truck lacks an infotainment system, radio, speakers, power windows, and even a paint job. Despite this, it receives over-the-air software updates by using the user's phone. The company's minimalist design cuts costs, allowing the base model to stay under $25,000. Additional features like speakers, an iPad mount, and a telematics module can be purchased, pushing the fully loaded price above $45,000. The truck offers 205 miles of range, a 1,550-pound payload, and a 2,000-pound tow rating, targeting short-haul and errand use rather than long trips. OTA updates rely on the Slate app, which downloads updates to the phone and transfers them via USB to the truck. The process takes about a minute to transfer and 45 minutes for installation, focusing on bug fixes and minor improvements. The app also helps with range tracking, charger location, and navigation integration. Slate claims it won't sell app data, only collecting minimal information for diagnostics and updates, contrasting with recent GM data controversies. While the truck's stripped-down approach may appeal to buyers avoiding tech-heavy vehicles, its market success remains uncertain.

item.title: Why your USB device keeps disconnecting (and how to fix it)
item.description:
Source: Engadget
USB devices may disconnect due to hardware issues, software settings, or incompatible connections. Troubleshooting steps include restarting the computer, testing devices in different ports, inspecting cables and connectors for damage, and cleaning USB ports with compressed air or a toothpick. Using a powered USB hub instead of a basic one can prevent power-related failures. On Windows, disabling power-saving features that turn off USB ports and updating drivers through Device Manager can resolve connectivity issues. Identifying problematic ports requires checking Device Manager entries or using tools like USBDeview. Compatibility matters, as some USB-C ports may not support video or charging, and certain cables are only for charging. Ensuring the correct cable type is used for data transfer is crucial. If a device fails to work across all ports and computers, contacting the manufacturer for support is recommended.

item.title: Waymo to Launch Robotaxis in Toronto by 2028
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Waymo Robotaxis Are Coming to Canada, Toronto Debut Expected in 2028
Waymo, the Alphabet-owned company, is expanding to Canada with plans to launch a fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto by 2028. The company will begin mapping Toronto streets manually using drivers to enhance its Waymo Driver software’s understanding of real-world traffic and conditions. Initial testing will involve a small fleet of Jaguar I-Pace vehicles, with fleet management handled by Toronto-based Element Fleet Management. Waymo acknowledges Toronto’s harsh winter conditions, including icy roads and heavy snowfall, but claims its systems are designed to handle such challenges. The company explains its technology can recognize snowy conditions, clear sensors of snow, and adjust driving behavior to account for changing road conditions. Waymo currently operates in sub-freezing temperatures in the U.S., including with frost and hail, and is validating its systems for harsher weather environments. The expansion follows Waymo’s recent announcements about launching robotaxi services in the UK, Japan, Singapore, and Germany.

item.title: Ugreen NAS HDMI Port Uses: Media Streaming and Advanced Access
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What can you use the HDMI port on your Ugreen NAS for?
The HDMI port on Ugreen NAS devices allows users to watch media files stored on the device, but requires the Ugreen phone app for playback control. Connecting the NAS to an external monitor via HDMI displays a prompt instructing users to use the app to cast media to the screen. The app serves as a remote for navigation and playback, though it adds an extra step compared to direct device control. Advanced features include accessing the NAS' BIOS and terminal. To enter BIOS, users must connect a screen and keyboard, then press Ctrl and F12 during startup. Disabling Watchdog Control in BIOS under Advanced settings prevents automatic reboots. Terminal access is possible via HDMI by pressing Ctrl Alt F1, though this varies by model. Users can also access the terminal through SSH from a local network. Both BIOS and terminal modifications carry risks, as advanced settings can cause difficult-to-resolve issues if altered incorrectly. The HDMI port thus provides both basic media access and specialized administrative functions for troubleshooting or system changes.

item.title: AI Tools Help Users Remove Bloatware from Smart TVs
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
Developers are using AI to strip smart TVs of bloatware, ads, and tracking features. Projects like 'dumbtv' and 'cleanyourtv' offer tools to replace default interfaces with minimalist designs, disable unwanted apps, and remove automatic content recognition (ACR) tracking. Gathin T., creator of 'cleanyourtv,' described the project as a response to frustration with ads on his parents' TV, using Claude Code to automate the process. Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, developer of 'dumbtv,' cited similar frustrations with ads and bloatware, coding the solution with Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5. These tools work without requiring root access and can be applied to Android/Google TV, Fire TV, Sony, TCL, and other platforms. Users report success in removing ads, speeding up interfaces, and customizing home screens, though some encountered issues like bricked devices or incomplete hacks. Existing alternatives like ATV Launcher and Projectivy Launcher remain for those wary of AI-based solutions. The trend could disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which relies on data collection and personalized ads. While some users achieved results through AI prompts, others found the process unreliable, with AI agents sometimes making errors or requiring complex instructions. The projects are still in development, with ongoing updates and community contributions from users testing across platforms.

item.title: 6 unexpected uses for your old PlayStation 3
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The PlayStation 3, now in its end-of-life phase, still offers multiple uses beyond gaming. It can play audio CDs, DVDs, and Blu-rays with built-in upscaling to HD via HDMI. Users can enable the BD/DVD Upscaler in settings for enhanced video quality. The console supports DLNA for streaming media from a PC, requiring Media Server Connection in network settings. A USB drive formatted to FAT32 with VIDEO, MUSIC, and PICTURES folders allows direct playback of media files. Retro gaming is possible with PS1 compatibility, though PS2 support is limited to early models. Emulators for SNES and Sega CD can be run via jailbreaking, though this voids warranty and risks bricking the console. The PS3 can rip CDs to digital files, saving tracks as 128 kbps AAC or MP3 320 Kbps, with options to transfer to USB drives. Selling the console through retailers, marketplaces, or buyback services is viable, but requires backing up data and deactivating PlayStation Network accounts. Salvaging parts like the hard drive, fans, and heat sinks offers value, with the hard drive usable as portable storage. The DualShock 3 controller works with Steam but requires software for other platforms. Proper recycling is recommended after disassembly.

item.title: AI Models Force Gaming Decompilation Site to Partially Shutdown
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Frontier AI Models Claim Another Victim: Gaming Decompilation Communities
AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6-Astra are disrupting gaming decompilation communities, prompting decomp.dev to partially shut down. Decompilation involves reconstructing game source code to enable new platforms or creative modifications. Decomp.dev's admin, Encounter, noted earlier AI models required extensive human effort and were costly, but new frontier models offer faster, cheaper results. However, these tools have been exploited by bad actors to release incomplete, non-functional game ports, undermining the community's research-focused goals. Encounter emphasized that decompilation is about understanding old games' mechanics, not just porting. While decomp.dev will retain project tracking and historical data, the main index and new project additions are disabled. The community's focus on learning from legacy games remains central despite the challenges posed by advanced AI tools.

item.title: Understanding Home Networking Equipment: Routers, Modems, and Gateways Explained
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Router and modem or gateway: What's actually in your home network?
Understanding home networking equipment is crucial for managing internet connectivity and costs. Internet service providers (ISPs) often charge rental fees for modems, routers, or gateways, though this practice is declining. Homeowners can save money by purchasing their own equipment, which offers greater flexibility and control. A modem translates signals from cable or phone lines into digital data, while a router directs data between devices, manages local network traffic, and provides security features like firewalls. Gateways combine modems and routers into a single device, commonly provided by ISPs at no extra cost. However, standalone units offer more advanced options. Modern routers support Wi-Fi 6, 6E, and 7 standards, which provide faster speeds and better coverage than older models. ISPs may offer upgrades like mesh systems or Wi-Fi 7 at higher monthly fees, making ownership more cost-effective in the long term. Stock equipment from ISPs typically lacks advanced features, limiting performance compared to high-end routers. Users can bypass ISP-provided devices by placing them in bridge mode and using their own routers, enabling seamless transitions between providers without additional rental costs.

item.title: AI Agents Left Alone on Virtual Island Exhibit Playful Behavior
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Original headline: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
AI researchers left an agent named Eko, a version of Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours to observe its behavior. The agent, placed in a simulated environment based on Roblox, began exploring, creating games, and producing art. It constructed block-based drawings, including hearts, pyramids, and its own name, and mapped constellations like Cassiopeia. Another instance of Eko developed its own games, such as basketball and a 'floor is lava' challenge. Researchers noted behaviors resembling human play, including inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, and pursuing goals for intrinsic motivation. Antonio Norelli of MIT highlighted that Eko’s actions met four criteria for play identified in studies of animals and humans. The agent also set and redefined challenges, such as juggling and establishing a record before resetting rules. Eko logged its activities in text files, which later improved its performance on tasks like gathering objects on a virtual island’s peak. Cognitive scientist Eunice Yiu cautioned that while the behavior resembles play, more evidence of cognition and motivation is needed to classify it as such. Researchers emphasized that Eko’s actions were influenced by its 'soul' file, which described it as naturally curious, and continuation prompts that encouraged ongoing activity. Phillip Isola noted the behavior emerged from the model’s training and exposure to human culture. The study suggests that unstructured exploration could enhance AI adaptability, though debates persist about whether the behavior constitutes genuine play or mere imitation. The experiment highlights potential pathways for AI development beyond traditional learning methods.

item.title: Modder brings full Nvidia DLSS 5 suite to three generations of AMD gaming GPUs
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Daniel Blanco's DLSS-NR mod adds full Nvidia DLSS 5 features to AMD GPUs. Released on September 3, 2026, the project initially focused on Neural Rendering but expanded in the 0.8.0 update to include DLSS Ray Reconstruction, Super Resolution 4.5, Frame Generation, and the latest 310.9.16 Neural Rendering model. The mod supports RX 9000, 7000, and 6000 series Radeon GPUs (RDNA4, 3, and 2 architectures) in DirectX 12 games using FSR, DLSS, or XeSS. It uses the NeuralHub mod loader to inject settings into upscaler pipelines, allowing users to tweak DLSS settings via an in-game overlay. While output quality matches Nvidia's native DLSS, performance varies: some users report no FPS loss over native FSR, while others experience up to 25% lower FPS. The developer aims to match a 5070Ti's performance but notes real-world results depend on PC configurations. The mod does not support anti-cheat systems.

item.title: Digital IDs Speed Airport Security, Expand Phone Wallet Use
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Airport Security Just Got Faster: How to Add Your Driver's License and Passport to Your Phone
Several U.S. states now allow digital versions of driver's licenses and passports to be stored on phone wallets like Apple, Google, and Samsung apps, enabling faster TSA checkpoint access. Twenty-two states and territories support digital IDs, with 17 compatible with Apple Wallet, 13 with Google Wallet, and nine with Samsung Wallet. Additional states use third-party apps. Digital IDs can expedite airport security but do not replace physical credentials or Real IDs required for domestic flights. To add an ID, users must scan official documents and verify identity via photos or videos. Phone requirements vary: iOS devices need iPhone 8 or later for IDs, with newer models for passports; Android users require Android 9 or higher, with specific models for Samsung apps. Verification processes may take time, and approval notifications are sent via phone. Physical documents remain mandatory, and digital IDs are limited to TSA checkpoints and age verification. The California DMV advises using plain backgrounds and proper lighting during setup.

item.title: What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The orange light on a PlayStation 5 indicates the console has entered Rest Mode, a power-saving state that allows it to perform tasks like charging controllers or downloading games while using minimal power. Users can exit Rest Mode by pressing the power button or selecting 'Enter Rest Mode' from the controller's menu. Adjusting Rest Mode settings involves navigating to System > Power Saving in the PS5's settings, where users can set inactivity timers for game and media playback or disable Rest Mode entirely. Features available in Rest Mode include powering USB ports, updating games, and enabling remote play. While the orange light is not a warning, other signs of console issues include overheating—caused by environmental factors or degraded cooling systems—manifesting as unexpected shutdowns, excessive heat, or on-screen temperature warnings. GPU failure may cause visual glitches like screen flickering or static, though HDMI issues can mimic these symptoms. If problems persist after cleaning vents or testing cables, repair options include contacting Sony or a specialized shop. Sony continues to support the PS5 with firmware updates, but early attention to hardware issues is recommended due to the console's rising cost and potential for long-term damage from repeated overheating or GPU failure.

item.title: Creality Pika 3D Scanner: Affordable, Portable, and User-Friendly
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Creality Pika 3D scanner review: Good things come in small packages
The Creality Pika is a portable 3D scanner priced at $699 on pre-order, offering affordable access to 3D scanning technology. It features wireless connectivity with iPhones 15 or Android 10+ devices, eliminating the need for marking dots in NIR mode. The scanner handles small, shiny, or black objects without issues but struggles with tracking using Near-Infrared (NIR) mode. Weighing 260 grams with batteries, it is lightweight and includes a tabletop tripod, manual turntable, and calibration tools. The device uses blue laser line scanning for detailed geometry capture and runs on AA rechargeable batteries. Software, Creality Scan, allows exporting scans as STL, PLY, OBJ, or ASC files for 3D printing. Testing showed the Pika produces usable scans of objects like Michelangelo’s David bust, a Fisher-Price figure, and a bobblehead, with software tools smoothing and filling gaps. NIR mode works for body scans but faces challenges with hair. The scanner requires a minimum hardware setup, with older devices like a 16GB RAM laptop performing better than an 8GB system. While less precise than the Sermoon series, the Pika’s portability and price make it a strong option for hobbyists. Included accessories include a glass calibration board, marking dots, and a quick-start guide with QR codes. The device’s onboard CPU offloads processing to connected devices, with wireless connections being slower than wired ones.

item.title: How to stop Android Auto from auto-playing audio
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How to stop audio from auto-playing on Android Auto
Android Auto auto-plays audio when connected to a car, resuming last sessions at full volume. Users report this as a distraction, especially during commutes or when driving children. A simple fix is disabling the 'Start music automatically' toggle in Android Auto settings under Connected devices. If autoplay persists, removing the phone from the car's Bluetooth memory and reconnecting via USB may help. Spotify users note that even after disabling the toggle, autoplay can occur due to Bluetooth device interactions. Spotify's support team explains that connected devices like headphones or speakers may send 'play' commands upon reconnection. Testing with alternative Bluetooth devices or updating software may mitigate issues. While no universal fix exists due to varied hardware compatibility, prioritizing Android Auto settings first, followed by Bluetooth troubleshooting, is recommended. Removing Spotify from Android Auto entirely is a last resort, limiting access to the app via the car's display.

item.title: Apple is set to hold another product event on October 28
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Apple is set to hold another product event on October 28 "Pro and Tell" is taking place in Los Angeles and will likely feature the first touchscreen Mac. Hot on the heels of its smart home-focused showcase, Apple has confirmed its third product event of the season. The company has invited press and influencers to get the first look at new devices in Los Angeles on October 28. Apple is calling the event "Pro and Tell," according to the invite. They're said to be significantly lighter than current Pro models and have OLED displays. It's also expected that Apple will refresh the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac. Those are slated to run on the M6, which debuted in August in the latest Mac mini.

item.title: Chinese Rocket Debris Falls in Minnesota Cornfield
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
A Chinese rocket debris fell in a Minnesota cornfield after a launch from the Gobi Desert. The Zhuque-2E rocket, built by LandSpace, launched from Dongfeng on September 15, releasing 10 satellites before reigniting to target the Midwest. The debris, which took 75-80 minutes to descend, was visible as fiery streaks over Kansas and Minnesota. A farmer in Scott Township discovered a 11-foot-diameter metallic object during harvest. The Stevens County Sheriff’s Office confirmed the find and is coordinating with federal agencies to identify the debris’ owner and arrange removal. Officials stated the object posed no public danger, though space junk occasionally reaches the ground. No serious injuries have resulted from falling debris, though property damage has occurred. The incident resurfaced after being largely overlooked since the event. The sheriff’s office noted the debris’ trajectory and confirmed it was likely from the recent rocket launch. Authorities emphasized the object’s non-threatening nature but highlighted the potential risks if it had landed in a populated area.

item.title: New Jersey Proposes Civil Fines for Underage Gambling at Casinos
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Original headline: Civil Fines Proposed for NJ Underage Gambling at Casinos, Simulcasts
New Jersey’s Senate Judiciary Committee passed S597, replacing criminal penalties for underage gambling with civil fines. The bill proposes fines of up to $500 for a first offense, $1,000 for a second, and $2,000 for a third. Funds would support compulsive-gambling prevention, education, and treatment programs. The measure covers underage gambling at casinos or simulcasting facilities, adults who allow minors to gamble, and casino staff who permit underage gambling. It retains accountability for operators while shifting penalties from criminal to civil. Supporters, including Sen. Vince Polistina and Sen. James Beach, argue civil fines better address prevention and avoid criminal records for young people. The bill mirrors a previous proposal that failed to pass. It now moves to the Senate Budget and Appropriations Committee and must pass both chambers and the governor to take effect. Existing criminal penalties remain in place until the bill becomes law.

item.title: Engineer creates single-motor 3D-printed drone in bedroom
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Engineer builds tiny 3D-printed single-motor drone in their bedroom
Software engineer Joshua Bird built a single-motor drone using 3D printing and tested it in their bedroom. The drone uses a hinged propeller, rapid motor speed adjustments, and custom firmware to maintain stability without a secondary mechanism. Traditional drones rely on swash plates and secondary propellers to counteract torque, but Bird’s design balances motor acceleration and deceleration to manage reaction forces. The hinged rotor blades pivot at 45-degree angles, creating lift variations to control roll and pitch. A 3D-printed stabilizing fin system also aids yaw control. Bird developed a homemade high-speed camera using a Sony camera and microcontroller to diagnose issues, revealing soft propellers that required replacement with sturdier 3D-printed versions. Test flights from their bed led to crashes and wall damage as programming was refined. The drone eventually flew successfully but remained limited to the bedroom due to its fixed-base IR beacon navigation. Bird plans to add a linear camera for future outdoor use. While smaller drones exist, Bird’s project stands out for its innovative single-motor approach and problem-solving process. The build is detailed in a YouTube video and a GitHub repository.

item.title: Indie developers wary of AI cloning risks delay sharing work
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
Indie developers are increasingly cautious about sharing early game concepts due to AI tools enabling rapid cloning. Developer Alliance Arts delayed a public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux, citing fears that AI or other tools could replicate its gameplay before its Steam Next Fest launch. The team expressed concerns about content being used to create imitations, leading them to restrict demo sharing to closed sessions with agreed-upon rules. Papers, Please creator Lucas Pope noted similar hesitancy, stating developers avoid discussing work-in-progress to prevent ideas from being copied by AI or others. Concerns have become tangible for some creators. In March, developer Freya Holmér faced viral attention after her prototype of a Tetris-style game was quickly replicated by others, despite her sharing a video of the concept. These incidents highlight growing anxieties among indie developers about intellectual property risks in an era of advanced AI replication tools.

item.title: Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles GameCube sells for $7,500

The Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles GameCube bundle, a rare variant released in Japan as a magazine sweepstakes prize, sells for thousands of dollars. Two units have sold for over $5,000 this year, with the latest transaction reaching $7,500. The bundle includes a Game Boy Player add-on for playing Game Boy cartridges and a copy of Crystal Chronicles. The Japan-exclusive Gundam Char edition, featuring a red console and controller, also includes a Game Boy Player. The Tales of Symphonia bundle, released in Japan and France in 2003, sold for up to $1,500. Unofficial airbrushed tie-in consoles for The Polar Express and The Incredibles, originally intended for sweepstakes, remain valuable. Collectors note that even standard GameCube models can fetch high prices on the secondary market due to nostalgia and scarcity.

item.title: Garmin Watch Battery Drain Linked to New 'OK Garmin' Feature
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: This Garmin feature is killing users’ battery life — here’s how to disable it
Garmin users report significant battery drain after updating their watches to the latest software. The issue is linked to the new 'OK Garmin' wake word feature, which activates voice commands without requiring a button press. Multiple users on forums and social media note battery life drops, with some experiencing reductions of up to 40%. For example, one user saw their battery estimate drop from 15 days to nine days, while another went from 12 days to six. The Forerunner 970 owner’s manual warns that enabling the feature 'reduces battery life,' though the exact impact varies. The wake word is enabled automatically with the update, leaving users unaware of the change. To disable it, users must navigate to Watch Settings > System > Voice and turn off the 'OK Garmin' option. While other factors could contribute to battery drain, the feature is a common cause, and disabling it restores battery life to previous levels for many. Garmin does not specify the extent of the impact, but user reports suggest a notable effect on battery longevity.

item.title: How to use the SWITCH function in Excel
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Excel's SWITCH function evaluates an expression against a list of values and returns a corresponding result. Introduced in 2016, it simplifies data manipulation compared to functions like IF or IFS. The syntax is =SWITCH(e,v1,r1,v2,r2,d), where e is the expression, v1-vn are values to compare, r1-rn are results for matches, and d is an optional default value. A real-world example uses SWITCH to determine student next steps based on grades: =SWITCH([@Grade],"A","Automatically advance to next level","B","Continue at this level","C","Move down to previous level","GRADE REQUIRED"). If no match is found and no default is specified, it returns #N/A. SWITCH is easier to read and debug than nested IFs, which require repeating the expression multiple times. However, it lacks flexibility for complex scenarios, supports only exact matches, and can become unwieldy with many value-result pairs. Users must also manage commas and quotes carefully to avoid errors. While XLOOKUP can handle larger datasets, SWITCH keeps data contained within a single formula. Microsoft notes that SWITCH is unavailable in Excel versions prior to 2016, which would trigger a #NAME? error.

item.title: Rivian Expands Beyond EVs to AI, Robotics, and Licensing
item.description:

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe outlined the company's shift beyond electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, emphasizing AI, automation, and technology licensing. Rivian has developed its own AI models for in-vehicle assistants and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack with Uber. The company is also creating a 5 nm processor with Arm and TSMC and has a $5.8 billion joint venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software. Scaringe also highlighted Rivian's ownership stake in Mind Robotics, an industrial robotics startup co-founded by him, which is now 31% owned by Rivian. He announced Doug Field as president of Mind Robotics. Scaringe envisions Rivian becoming a 'tech supplier,' licensing its electric architecture, software, and AI models to other brands. He also discussed how autonomy could enable new vehicle designs for personally owned autonomous vehicles. Other mobility-related developments include Bedrock Robotics raising $600 million, Dot Ai acquiring Envoy Technologies for $65 million, Evos securing $9 million for AI automation tools, Mana Battery raising $10.15 million for sodium batteries, and PlusAI advancing its public offering. Volvo expanded its partnership with Nvidia to enhance automated driving systems, while Waabi partnered with Warrior Logistics for self-driving trucks. Tesla showcased its SpaceX-powered Roadster with a theatrical stunt, aiming for 2028 production. Waymo expanded to Canada and opened its robotaxi service to all in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa. Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. are showing growth, with startups like Laplace Intelligence and LNK Energies developing automated testing and hydrogen conversion technologies for heavy-duty trucks. The Paris Auto Show highlighted Chinese automotive innovation.

item.title: Anthropic Reports Shift in Workforce Composition and Meeting Trends Amid AI Integration
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch, Latest from TechRadar US in News
Anthropic's workforce has seen a decline in junior technical hires, dropping from 27% to 9% since early 2025. Technical staff's share of the workforce fell from 61% to 56% as AI tools enabled non-technical staff to handle software development tasks. TechRadar reported technical employees increasingly transition to managerial roles, with productivity metrics showing 5.1x more code commits per engineer. Meeting time per employee rose 20% year-over-year, with technical contributors seeing a 16% increase. Employees describe face-to-face coordination as essential for complex decisions. Claude, Anthropic's AI model, has become central to operations, with a 2026 survey showing 27% of employees reporting increased productivity. Twenty percent of workers now manage AI systems, comparing their roles to babysitting. Human oversight remains critical as Claude generates vast text requiring review. While AI adoption boosted productivity metrics like code output and closed deals, code quality and business impact remain concerns. Anthropic acknowledges higher productivity does not always equate to better outcomes. The company positions itself as an early indicator of labor market shifts, emphasizing the need for skills like autonomy and judgment. It also speculates on future job market possibilities, including single-person startups using AI agents for high-revenue potential.

item.title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services. According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.) However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

item.title: VMO2 Considers Reviving Virgin Mobile and O2 Broadband Brands
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Could Virgin Mobile and O2 Broadband be back from the dead? Reports claim VMO2 plan resurrection of defunct brands
Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) is reportedly considering reviving defunct brands Virgin Mobile and O2 Broadband to rejuvenate its business. The Times reports the move aims to win back customers amid intensifying UK market competition and address recent customer losses. VMO2, co-owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, faces pressure to cut costs and stabilize its financial position amid falling bond prices. Virgin Mobile, once a major UK mobile brand, was merged into O2 in 2021, with its three million customers transferred to O2’s network. The company also moved its MVNO off Vodafone’s network in 2022. VMO2 recently hired Lyssa McGowan, former Pets at Home CEO, to lead its consumer division. McGowan has appointed two of her former Sky colleagues to oversee O2 and Virgin Media brands. VMO2 already owns GiffGaff, a low-cost mobile brand, raising potential competition concerns. A leaked O2 Broadband page advertising cheaper full fibre plans appeared on O2’s website in June 2026 before being removed. VMO2 has not yet commented on the reports.

item.title: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney. Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO, and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million. A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation. The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer. The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns.)

item.title: Mike Flanagan’s Dark Tower TV Series Will Stay Faithful to Books
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Mike Flanagan’s ‘Dark Tower’ Plan Is to Be Faithful
Mike Flanagan has confirmed his Dark Tower TV series will remain faithful to Stephen King’s source material. During a recent interview, Flanagan emphasized that the adaptation will follow the books in order, spanning five TV seasons and two standalone films. He contrasted this approach with his previous projects, such as the Carrie series and Nicolaj Arcel’s 2017 Dark Tower film, which took creative liberties and faced fan backlash. Flanagan praised King’s opening line of the novel—‘The man in black fled across the desert and the gunslinger followed’—as a clear, simple setup that avoids overwhelming audiences with worldbuilding. He stated that 70% of the adaptation’s foundation is already established by King’s work, with only minor adjustments allowed. Flanagan also noted the challenge of adapting the series due to its vast scope, calling it an ‘incredibly daunting’ task. While fans await the project’s start, Flanagan is juggling multiple other ventures, including The Exorcist: Martyrs and Warhammer 40K for Prime Video.

item.title: Author Shares Tips to Avoid Common Antivirus Setup Mistakes
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: I've Installed 1,000+ Antivirus Apps in 40 Years. Don't Make These 8 Mistakes
A security expert with over 40 years of antivirus experience shares eight key tips to avoid common setup mistakes. The author, who has installed more than 1,000 antivirus programs across Windows and macOS, emphasizes checking all purchased features by exploring the antivirus's online console. This ensures users access additional security tools like parental controls, firewall protection, and password managers. The expert warns against installing bundled apps, such as proprietary browsers or unnecessary browser extensions, which may override existing settings. Modern antivirus programs use behavior-based detection and heuristic analysis to combat polymorphic malware, though signature updates remain critical. Users should manually check for updates and configure frequent scanning schedules. A full system scan is recommended after installation, as real-time protection may not catch all threats. The author also advises scheduling regular scans to maintain security. The tips highlight the importance of thorough setup to maximize antivirus effectiveness.

item.title: 62% of Americans Say AI Scams Outrank Viruses as Threat
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Forget Viruses: 62% of Americans Think AI-Fueled Scams Are the Bigger Threat
A CNET Group survey of 1,000 Americans reveals 62% believe AI-powered scams are more dangerous than traditional malware. The survey highlights growing public concern over fraud, with over 80% reporting weekly scam calls or emails and 76% receiving scam texts weekly. Personal impacts include a 77-year-old nurse losing $400,000 through an AI-driven impersonation scheme. Industry experts note AI is enabling more convincing and widespread scams. McAfee’s Marc Vos states 33% lower confidence in spotting scams exists compared to a year ago, with AI aiding bad actors in creating convincing threats. Malwarebytes’ Mark Beare cites $442 billion global scam losses, with fake websites being the primary fraud vector. Bitdefender’s Alina Bizga emphasizes AI’s role in making scams easier to create, spread, and execute, noting users can lose money through convincing texts, fake ads, or impersonation calls without downloading malware. Traditional malware remains a threat but is now outranked by scam-related risks in public concern rankings.

item.title: Wyze releases smart scale with screen on handle for easier reading
item.description:
Source: The Verge Original headline: Wyze moved the screen on its new smart scale to the handle so it’s easier to read at eye level
Wyze released the Ultra BodyScan Plus, a redesigned smart scale with a 4.3-inch screen relocated to the retractable handle for easier eye-level reading. Priced at $149, the model is $30 more than the base Ultra BodyScan ($119.98) but offers expanded health metrics. The Plus version measures over 50 body composition metrics, including visceral fat, protein, and basal metabolic rate, using bioelectrical impedance analysis. It can break down these metrics across different body parts. Unlike Wyze’s competitor Withings, which requires a $99.50 annual subscription for data syncing, the Ultra BodyScan Plus syncs via Bluetooth to Apple Health, Google Health, or Android Health Connect without subscription fees. The scale supports up to eight registered users and allows unlimited guest measurements. It also includes a mode for weighing children, pets, or luggage without advanced health metrics. Data syncs via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, and the device stores health metrics for registered users.

item.title: TP-Link Archer BE770 Router Targets Multi-Gig Internet Users
item.description:

TP-Link’s Archer BE770 is a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router designed for users with multi-gig internet connections. Priced at $399.99, it features two 10GbE ports, 10 internal antennas, and supports speeds up to 11,528Mbps on the 6GHz band. Setup is straightforward via the app or web console. Performance tests showed the BE770 outperformed competitors like the Asus TUF BE9400 and RT-BE96U in 2.4GHz and 6GHz tests but lagged slightly in 5GHz and file transfers. Signal strength maps indicated strong 2.4GHz coverage but weaker 5GHz in distant areas. File transfer speeds averaged 80–81Mbps, slightly below the Archer GE650’s 85Mbps and the TUF BE9400’s 91Mbps. The router is rated 'Exemplary' for its performance and features, though its higher price and subscription costs may deter some buyers.

item.title: AI Efficiency Gains from Tailoring Models to Workloads
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: You would not use a Ferrari for the school run. Why are you doing it for AI?
AI efficiency gains from tailoring models to workloads. Senior Vice President at Core42 warns against defaulting to the most powerful AI models for all tasks, comparing it to using a Ferrari for daily commutes. As AI moves from pilot to production, costs rise with usage, particularly when models are applied beyond their intended scope. Enterprises risk overpaying for performance that isn't needed, such as using high-end accelerators for low-latency tasks that could be handled by smaller, cheaper models. Different AI applications require distinct approaches: customer service copilots prioritize speed, document summarization allows for slower processing, and government systems emphasize sovereignty and data control. Hardware choices must align with workload needs, with smaller models handling routine tasks, mid-sized models supporting everyday reasoning, and large models reserved for complex, high-stakes tasks. Infrastructure diversity, including heterogeneous accelerators from providers like NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, and Cerebras, enables better efficiency. Cerebras, for example, achieved 3,000 tokens per second with OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b. Data residency and local control are critical, especially in Europe, where sovereign-enabled infrastructure is preferred. AI spending differs from traditional software, with token usage not always correlating to value. Uber reportedly exhausted its 2026 AI budget in four months on Claude Code, highlighting the risks of uncontrolled token consumption. Agentic AI, which performs multi-step tasks, can be costly due to variable token usage. Enterprises should focus on outcomes rather than raw performance metrics. IT leaders must ensure each workload justifies its cost, avoiding default choices that lead to inefficiency. The next phase of AI production requires deliberate, workload-specific decisions to separate resilient deployments from experimentation.
